subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: reacting to each crisis as it comes [Pitfall]
passage: Chetan's phone buzzed in the middle of the quarterly review. He glanced at it, went pale, and stood. "Sorry. My father has fallen again." Naveen, chairing the meeting, nodded. It was the third such dash out of the office this month, and the client presentation Chetan owned still had gaps. Later, at the coffee machine, Naveen said gently, "I'm not upset about your father. But I can't plan around it. Do you have a backup? Someone who can go instead?" Chetan opened his mouth. There was no name he could give. His sister was in another city, and the neighbour had never been asked. Naveen said nothing more, but Chetan saw a colleague quietly take over his slides. He went home worried, not only about his father, but about how he was being seen.

qa.q: How many times had Chetan dashed out of the office that month?
qa.a: It was the third such dash out of the office that month.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on the way home, and why?
qa.a: Chetan felt worried about his father and about how his colleagues were seeing him.

qa.q: What would a better plan look like for Chetan?
qa.a: It would include a named backup person, emergency contacts, and a talk with Naveen about cover, so a crisis does not mean rushing out each time.

qa.q: How might Naveen see the repeated absences?
qa.a: Naveen may feel sympathetic but stuck, since without a backup plan the team cannot plan around the interruptions.

grounding: Chetan rushes out of work for each fall with no plan, damaging his reputation and leaving no backup.

subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: reacting to each crisis as it comes [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Jyoti,

You asked why I sounded so rattled on the phone. Here is the honest version.
Since Papa's first fall in January, I've had no plan. When the neighbour calls to say he's fallen, I run out of the office. When Mummy's sugar goes up and she needs the hospital, I run out again. Six times in four months, each time with no notice.
Last week my manager said, quite kindly, that the team can't depend on me for the client launch. They've given it to someone else. I've heard people call me "the one who disappears".
And the worst part: when I was in Delhi for a two-day training, Papa fell again, and there was nobody. The neighbour sat with him for three hours until I found an auto driver to take them to the clinic.
We need a real plan, Jyoti, and I can't make it alone. Can we talk this Sunday?

Pankaj

qa.q: How many times did Pankaj leave the office suddenly in four months?
How is Pankaj feeling, and what shows it?
qa.a: Pankaj feels rattled and ashamed, hearing colleagues use the nickname "the one who disappears" and losing the client launch.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Pankaj better than reacting to each crisis?
qa.a: Pankaj and Jyoti could make a plan with emergency contacts, a nearby hospital, a spare key with a neighbour and some regular help, so there is backup when he is away.

qa.q: How is Papa affected by the lack of a plan?
qa.a: When Pankaj was away, Papa had to wait three hours after a fall with only the neighbour, showing the family had no backup.

grounding: It shows someone with no plan rushing out of the office for each fall or hospital visit, damaging their reputation and leaving the family with no backup.

subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: reacting to each crisis as it comes [Pitfall]
passage:
Usha, you asked why I got passed over for team lead. I'll tell you, since you're dealing with your own parents now. I'm Kiran, and last year I was the king of last-minute leave.
My mother has heart trouble, and my father's memory is going. We had no plan at all. Every time something happened, I'd get a call and just run: grab my bag in the middle of a meeting, half-finished work left on my desk.
It happened maybe ten times. Each time felt like the right thing. It was my mother!
But my manager said, at my review, "I never know if you'll be here tomorrow." The lead role went to someone else.
And the worst part is, one day I was stuck in traffic on the highway when my father wandered out, and there was nobody else to call. My neighbour found him two hours later.
So please, Usha. Make a plan before you need it.

qa.q: What did Kiran's manager say at the review?
qa.a: "I never know if you'll be here tomorrow."

qa.q: How does Kiran feel looking back on that year?
qa.a: Kiran feels regretful and shaken, especially about the day the father wandered out and there was nobody else to call.

qa.q: What else could Kiran have done instead of running out at each crisis?
qa.a: Kiran could have made an emergency plan with backup contacts, a neighbour with a key and regular help, and told the manager about it in advance.

qa.q: How might Kiran's manager have seen the repeated last-minute leave?
qa.a: The manager likely felt unable to rely on Kiran for important work, which is why the lead role went to someone else.

grounding: It shows someone with no plan rushing from work at every crisis, which damages their reputation and leaves the family without backup.
